titre: Drinking the Proof of an Ulcer
accroche: In 1984, an Australian doctor drinks a bacterial culture to prove that stress is not the cause of ulcers
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1984, in a laboratory in Perth, a 32-year-old doctor swallows the contents of a bacterial culture dish. He is not sick: he is trying to become so, to prove a point that no one wants to hear.

## The Dogma That Had to Be Broken

For decades, medicine has explained stomach ulcers by stress, gastric acidity, and spices. Treatment follows this logic: rest, diet, antacids, never antibiotics, since no bacterium, it is believed, can survive in an environment as acidic as the stomach.

In 1979, however, the pathologist J. Robin Warren observes, on a gastric biopsy, spiral-shaped bacteria nestled against the stomach wall. Barry Marshall, a young trainee in gastroenterology, takes over the follow-up of his patients in 1981. Together they find the same bacterium, later named Helicobacter pylori, in nearly all patients suffering from duodenal or gastric ulcers, and publish it in *The Lancet* as early as 1983.

Publishing is not enough: the medical community remains skeptical, for lack of a demonstrated cause-and-effect link in humans rather than in dish cultures.

## Drinking the Proof

Marshall then decides to meet for himself the standards of proof being demanded of him. On a July morning in 1984, he drinks a cloudy broth containing the bacterium taken from a patient. For the first three days, no symptoms, other than a feeling of fullness after the evening meal. Then, between the fifth and eighth days, nausea and morning vomiting set in, to the point that his wife points out that his breath has become foul. A follow-up endoscopy, ten days after ingestion, shows a well-established acute gastritis, exactly the lesion he claimed the bacterium caused. The symptoms subside in fourteen days, without his having taken any antibiotic.

The experiment, published in an Australian medical journal, does not immediately convince the profession. It will take ten more years, and a consensus conference of the U.S. health institutes in February 1994, for the link between H. pylori and ulcers to be officially recognized. Antibiotics then become the standard treatment, in place of diet and rest.

## What This Shifts

Warren and Marshall receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005. The jury's announcement is blunt: the bacterium causes more than 90% of duodenal ulcers and up to 80% of gastric ulcers, and badly digested stress has almost nothing to do with it.

The shift does not stop at gastroenterology. Solid evidence is not always enough to change a long-established medical consensus. It took proof that strikes the imagination, at personal risk to the person producing it, to speed up what a scientific paper alone had not achieved. Since then, Marshall's self-experiment has become a textbook case, cited as a radical and rarely imitated way of short-circuiting the inertia of an entire discipline.

citation.texte: This was one of those occasions when it would be easier to get forgiveness than permission.

carte.punch: He drank a bacterial culture to prove that ulcers are not a matter of stress.
carte.idee: In 1984, Barry Marshall swallows a culture of the bacterium later named Helicobacter pylori and develops gastritis. In February 1994, a U.S. consensus conference recognizes the link with ulcers. Nobel 2005: it causes more than 90% of duodenal ulcers, stress almost none.

quiz.question: Why did Marshall's self-experiment in 1984 matter more than his earlier scientific publications?
choix: Because it demonstrated a cause-and-effect link in humans, not only in dish cultures
Because it immediately convinced the entire medical community
Because it made it possible to discover the bacterium for the first time
Because it proved that stress aggravates existing ulcers
quiz.explication: Warren and Marshall had already published the statistical link between the bacterium and ulcers; what was missing was proof of a cause-and-effect link in human beings. Official recognition came only ten years later, and the experiment never concerned the aggravation of existing ulcers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long did it take, after Marshall's self-experiment in 1984, for the link between H. pylori and ulcers to be officially recognized?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The self-experiment dates from July 1984, and it took until the consensus conference of the U.S. health institutes in February 1994, about ten years later, for the link to be officially recognized and for antibiotics to become the standard treatment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the first sign Marshall felt after drinking the bacterial culture?
choix: A gastritis diagnosed by endoscopy on the very first day
A feeling of fullness after the evening meal
Violent vomiting within the first hours
A total loss of appetite lasting two weeks
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first three days showed no notable symptoms, other than a feeling of fullness after the evening meal; nausea and vomiting appeared only between the fifth and eighth days, and the endoscopy took place only ten days after ingestion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What observation did Warren make in 1979, before Marshall took over the follow-up of his patients?
choix: Spiral bacteria against the stomach wall, on a biopsy
A total resistance of certain bacteria to antibiotics
A vitamin B12 deficiency in ulcer patients
A congenital malformation of the stomach wall
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1979, the pathologist Warren observes, on a gastric biopsy, spiral-shaped bacteria nestled against the stomach wall, an observation that Marshall would take up and generalize starting in 1981.
